newsitem.title: USA: TWA victims remembered at memorial services.
newsitem.headline: TWA victims remembered at memorial services.

text.p: Several memorial services were planned Thursday for the 230 victims of TWA Flight 800, which blew up in mid-air and crashed into the sea off Long Island July 17 one year ago.
The cause of the disaster remains something of a mystery. Although investigators know the nearly empty but vapor-filled center fuel tank exploded, they have not determined exactly why.
Investigators say they strongly suspect the crash occurred because of a mechanical failure rather than sabotage by bomb or missile, two of the other main theories in the probe.

At one of Thursday's services in New York, relatives and friends of the victims from across the United States and overseas will attend a public memorial mass at St Patrick's Cathedral on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan.
In the afternoon, New York State Governor George Pataki will host a memorial service at Smith Point Park on Long Island near the site where the aircraft came down into the Atlantic Ocean.
Lead National Transportation Safety Board investigator Robert Francis and FBI assistant director James Kallstorm would be meeting families of the victims in the coming days.
Kallstrom said he felt "sadness and emotion about the tragedy, the unfulfilled lives". He said the affects of the catastrophe had galvanized investigators to find the cause.
Another service is planned Thursday in Montoursville, Pa., the home town of 16 high school French Club members and 5 adult chaperones who were among those who perished.

TWA Flight 800 exploded in mid-air without warning just 11 minutes after taking off from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport on a flight to Paris. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed.

Thursday's services and a memorial at the airport Wednesday for TWA Flight 800's crew were among many events scheduled over five days to remember those who died or to honor the hundreds of people from government agencies or volunteers who worked in the aftermath of the disaster.

A highlight of the TWA service was the unveiling of a six-foot high statue featuring three etched glass panels showing the plane taking off, being cupped gently in a pair of hands and then being transformed into a bird.
